subject: surgery
title: Topical Antimicrobials, Early Excision, and Post-Burn Contractures

steps.tx: Avascular thermal eschar prevents systemically administered intravenous antibiotics from reaching the infected burn wound surface in therapeutic concentrations. Consequently, daily application of effective topical antimicrobial agents forms the cornerstone of non-operative burn wound care. The most widely prescribed topical preparation is one percent **silver sulfadiazine** cream, valued for its broad-spectrum bactericidal activity against Gram-negative bacilli and Gram-positive staphylococci. Formulated in a soothing water-soluble base, it applies painlessly and does not alter systemic electrolyte concentrations.
steps.say: Because systemic antibiotics cannot penetrate avascular dead eschar, topical agents are vital. Silver sulfadiazine cream provides broad-spectrum bactericidal coverage without causing painful irritation on application.

vis.alt: Silver sulfadiazine cream applied daily to a burn wound as topical antimicrobial cover over avascular eschar
vis.caption: Silver sulfadiazine cream applied daily to a burn wound as topical antimicrobial cover over avascular eschar. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Clinicians utilizing silver sulfadiazine must remain vigilant for its classic pharmacological side effects and clinical limitations. A transient, self-limiting **neutropenia** with circulating white blood cell counts dropping below four thousand per microlitre characteristically emerges between the second and fourth days of therapy due to transient marrow marginalization. Furthermore, silver sulfadiazine reacts with wound exudate to form a tenacious, yellowish pseudo-eschar that hinders accurate clinical depth evaluation. The drug is contraindicated in patients with known sulfonamide hypersensitivity and in late pregnancy.
steps.say: Silver sulfadiazine can trigger a transient drop in white blood cell counts within the first four days of use. It also produces a yellowish pseudo-eschar that can obscure underlying wound depth.

steps.tx: When managing deep burns involving avascular cartilage such as the external ear or nasal framework, alternative topical formulations are required. Ten percent **mafenide acetate** cream diffuses rapidly through thick, leathery eschar, providing outstanding antimicrobial coverage against invasive Pseudomonas species. However, mafenide causes severe local stinging pain upon application and readily absorbs into the systemic circulation. Systemic absorption inhibits renal carbonic anhydrase, provoking impaired bicarbonate reabsorption, compensatory hyperventilation, and systemic hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis that can destabilize critically ill patients.
steps.say: Mafenide acetate penetrates deep eschar and cartilaginous structures effectively. However, it causes significant local pain and inhibits carbonic anhydrase, which can provoke metabolic acidosis.

steps.tx: Waiting for dead skin to declare itself went out of fashion when surgeons learned what early removal achieves. **Early excision** strips burn eschar within the first days, before bacteria colonise its avascular depths, and covers the wound while the patient still has physiological reserve to spend. Sepsis rates and hospital stays fell wherever the practice took hold. The image captures the philosophy shift: the eschar is not a dressing to be preserved but a liability whose removal, timed boldly, is itself the treatment.
steps.say: Early excision removes burn eschar before colonisation, cutting sepsis and shortening recovery.

steps.tx: Modern surgical burn care has shifted decisively away from prolonged conservative dressings toward active surgical intervention. Pioneered by Janzekovic, **early excision** entails the aggressive surgical debridement of non-viable, necrotic skin within the first twenty-four to seventy-two hours following initial hemodynamic stabilization. Prompt removal of non-viable tissue eliminates the primary bacterial culture medium, aborts the release of systemic inflammatory mediators, and markedly decreases the incidence of invasive burn wound sepsis, hospital duration, and overall patient mortality.
steps.say: Early surgical excision within seventy-two hours of injury eliminates devitalized tissue before severe bacterial colonization occurs. This timely intervention dramatically reduces systemic sepsis and shortens hospital stay.

vis.alt: Surgical photograph showing thorough wound debridement and preparation of a viable bed.
vis.caption: Surgical debridement and preparation of a healthy, vascularized recipient wound bed. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: During operative intervention, the surgical team performs sequential **tangential excision**, shaving thin layers of non-viable burn tissue using a specialized dermatome or Humby knife until a glistening, viable bed with brisk pinpoint capillary bleeding is encountered. Alternatively, deeply charred burns extending into subcutaneous fat undergo fascial excision, sacrificing subcutaneous tissue down to the investing deep fascia. Fascial debridement substantially reduces intraoperative blood loss and provides a reliably vascularized bed, but produces significant cosmetic disfigurement and secondary distal lymphatic drainage compromise.
steps.say: Tangential excision involves shaving thin layers of necrotic tissue until healthy, punctate capillary bleeding is reached. Deeper burns may require fascial excision, which sacrifices subcutaneous fat down to the deep fascia.

steps.tx: Immediately following satisfactory surgical debridement, the freshly excised wound bed must be sealed against desiccation and infection through immediate autografting or temporary biological coverage. When the available donor skin is insufficient to cover extensive body surface burns, harvested autologous split-thickness grafts undergo mechanical meshing. A specialized **meshed graft** expands the available surface area by ratios ranging from one point five to one up to three to one, while allowing underlying serous exudate to drain freely through the mesh apertures.
steps.say: Once excision is complete, immediate coverage is mandatory. Meshing harvested skin grafts multiplies their surface area and creates drainage slits that prevent fluid accumulation beneath the graft.

nodes.label: Sheet Autograft or Meshed Split Graft Placed

steps.tx: Prolonged healing by secondary intention across mobile joints or flexion creases inevitably results in severe, disabling scarring. Persistent activation of differentiated contractile myofibroblasts alongside aberrant collagen cross-linking produces a rigid **post-burn contracture**. These cicatricial bands cause profound functional limitation across the neck, axillae, antecubital fossae, popliteal spaces, and hands. Prevention requires meticulous positioning in anti-contracture extension, rigid splinting during nocturnal sleep, and early aggressive active physiotherapy initiated during acute inpatient recovery.
steps.say: Post-burn contractures develop when deep wounds heal with dense, myofibroblast-driven scar tissue across mobile joints. Preventive splinting in anti-contracture positions and early physical therapy are essential.

steps.tx: Once mature cicatricial contractures produce fixed functional impairment, surgical reconstruction becomes mandatory to restore joint range of motion. Operative management begins with complete surgical release or complete excision of the fibrous contracture band until full passive joint mobility is restored. The resulting soft tissue defect requires coverage with local transposition flaps, Z-plasties, or full-thickness skin grafts. Following successful surgical release, patients must wear custom-fabricated **pressure garments** delivering twenty-five millimetres of mercury continuously for up to eighteen months to prevent hypertrophic scar recurrence.
steps.say: Surgical release of mature contractures restores mobility, after which flaps or thick skin grafts cover the defect. Patients wear continuous pressure garments for many months to inhibit hypertrophic scar reformation.
